Vest supports three order types, **Market, Limit, and Scale,** with additional options like **Reduce Only, Take Profit, and Stop Loss.** All order types are available across every market and on both Primary Accounts and Funded Accounts.
Executes immediately at the best available price on the order book.
Use market orders when speed matters more than price precision. For example, when reacting to news or closing a position quickly.
Executes at your specified price or better. Execution is not guaranteed; the Time in Force determines whether an unfilled order rests or cancels.
Use limit orders when price certainty matters more than execution speed. Limit orders rest on the order book (subject to your Time in Force setting), or execute immediately if marketable.
Distributes a large order across a price range by placing multiple limit orders at graduated prices between a start price and an end price.

Scale orders reduce market impact for larger sizes and can improve average fill price when building or unwinding positions gradually. Configure the start price, end price, and number of orders to distribute across the range.

Market orders offer IOC or FOK and default to IOC. Limit and Scale orders offer GTC, IOC, FOK or ALO and default to GTC. IOC fills available size immediately and cancels the remainder. FOK fills the entire order immediately or cancels it without a partial fill. ALO is the post-only option.
Limit and Scale orders default to **GTC**.
Available modifiers depend on the order type. The entry TP/SL controls appear on Market and Limit forms, not on the Scale form.
Prevents the order from opening a new position in the opposite direction. If the order wouldn't reduce (or close) an existing position, it's rejected before submission.
Use Reduce Only when trimming or closing a position and you want to guarantee you don't accidentally flip your side by over-executing.
Orders that activate at a specified trigger price. The trigger is not a guaranteed fill price: market execution can slip, while a limit order may remain unfilled. Trading locks can prevent execution.
* **Take Profit** — closes the position at a specified profit level
* **Stop Loss** — closes the position at a specified loss level

Each can be set as either a **limit** or a **market** order, by your choice. Both can be attached at the time of order entry via the TP/SL toggle on Market and Limit order forms, or added to an open position later from the Portfolio.
Orders match against the resting order book at the best available price. Key mechanics:
* **Price-time priority** — best prices fill first; ties are broken by time of submission
* **Partial fills** — GTC orders may fill partially and leave the remainder resting; IOC fills available size and cancels the remainder. FOK is all-or-none and does not permit partial execution.
Fees are calculated per fill and vary by market.
The order form displays a **Fail Price** for Funded Account risk limits. On Primary Accounts, the corresponding risk label is Liq. Price (Mark), the estimated liquidation price.
Use Fail Price to check downside risk before submitting. If either side's Fail Price is uncomfortably close to the current market, adjust size or leverage before placing the order.

Vest uses a single, unified margin model across every account: **cross margin**, with leverage up to 100x depending on account type and market.

Margin lets you open positions larger than the collateral you've deposited. Instead of paying the full value of a position upfront, you post a fraction of it, the margin, and the rest is effectively borrowed exposure, backed by your account.

Leverage allows greater exposure relative to your equity, magnifying gains and losses relative to that equity. For a fixed position size and price move, dollar PnL is unchanged by the leverage setting.

Vest uses market units rather than CME contract counts. On ES and NQ, 1 Vest unit gains or loses 1 USDC for each 1-point price move. To match the price exposure of a futures position, multiply the number of CME contracts by the equivalent Vest quantity below.

For either index, 1 E-mini has the price exposure of 10 Micro E-minis. For example, 3 MES correspond to 15 ES units on Vest, and 3 MNQ correspond to 6 NQ units. These are gross price-exposure equivalents before fees and funding; Vest perpetuals have their own pricing, margin requirements, and trading rules. CME multipliers: [Micro E-mini contract specifications](https://www.cmegroup.com/articles/faqs/micro-e-mini-equity-index-futures-frequently-asked-questions.html).

Choose ES or NQ, then switch the Amount field from USDC to the market unit and enter the Vest quantity from the table. When Amount is set to USDC, it represents position notional, not the margin you are posting. Notional = quantity × price; estimated initial margin = notional ÷ leverage. Check the order preview for the resulting size, margin, fees, and estimated Fail Price where applicable.

At a hypothetical ES price of 6,000, enter 5 ES units for the price exposure of 1 MES. The position notional is 5 × 6,000 = 30,000 USDC. At 10x leverage, estimated initial margin is 3,000 USDC before fees. A 10-point rise produces 50 USDC of gross profit on a long position; a 10-point fall produces a 50 USDC loss. A short position has the opposite result.

Changing leverage changes the margin required for these 5 units, not their 5 USDC-per-point exposure. To estimate price risk, multiply quantity by the distance to your stop: 5 units × 20 points = 100 USDC before fees, funding, and slippage. A stop does not guarantee its execution price, and account loss limits apply to total equity across all open positions.
Leverage is set per market and displayed on that market's trading page.
* **Primary Accounts** — up to **100x**, market-dependent
* **Funded Accounts** — up to **50x**, market-dependent
Markets with lower liquidity or higher volatility typically cap leverage lower than highly liquid markets like BTC or major equity indices.
Primary (direct) and Funded Account maximum leverage is listed below. “Unavailable” means the market cannot be traded on Funded Accounts.

BTC and ETH have a 15x maximum on Funded Accounts. ES has a 75x maximum on both Primary and Funded Accounts. NQ and RTY have a 50x maximum on both Primary and Funded Accounts. HYPE and XRP are unavailable to trade on Funded Accounts.
Leverage is set per market from the trading view.
1. Open the market you want to trade.
2. Click the leverage indicator near the top of the order form (shows your current multiplier, e.g. "5x").
3. Use the slider or preset buttons to choose a new leverage level, up to that market's maximum.
4. Confirm the change.
The order-form leverage setting controls sizing for new orders. Effective portfolio leverage is a separate measure: total notional exposure divided by current portfolio equity.
Adding to a position changes total exposure. Effective portfolio leverage also changes when account equity changes, including through unrealized PnL.
Vest uses **cross margin** across every market. There is no isolated margin option.

Cross margin means your full account collateral backs all open positions simultaneously, rather than each position drawing from its own separate margin pool. Gains on one position can offset losses on another, which improves capital efficiency but also means positions are not risk-isolated from each other.
**Portfolio Value** is calculated as:
Portfolio Value = Collateral + Total Realized PnL + Total Unrealized PnL
**Portfolio Leverage** is calculated as:
Leverage = Total Notional Value / Portfolio Value
When you open a new position, your specified size adjusts the leverage across your entire portfolio — leverage is a portfolio-level figure, not something tracked independently per position.
**Isolated margin is not available on Vest.** All positions use cross margin, on every market, at every leverage level.
To open a new position, your portfolio value must meet the total initial margin requirement:
Total Initial Margin Requirement = Σ (Position Size × Index Price × Initial Margin Ratio)
If your portfolio value falls below this threshold, the trade will not execute.

The **maintenance margin requirement** works the same way but uses the maintenance margin ratio instead of the initial margin ratio. If your portfolio value drops below the maintenance threshold due to unrealized losses, liquidation occurs.
A simplified example to make the formulas concrete.
Say your account has:
* **Collateral:** $10,000
* **Total Realized PnL:** $0
* **Total Unrealized PnL:** −$200 (one open position is currently down $200)
Now say you're holding one position with a notional value of $50,000 (for example, 0.5 BTC at $100,000):

Your account is running approximately 5.102x portfolio leverage. Additional exposure increases the numerator; collateral, realized PnL and unrealized PnL can change the $9,800 portfolio value in the denominator.

On a Funded Account, leverage choice directly affects how quickly adverse price moves can bring your account to a risk-rule floor. Whether that's the **Max. Drawdown**, or, on evaluation-path accounts that carry one, the **Daily Loss Limit**. Higher leverage means a given percentage move in the underlying market produces a larger swing in portfolio value, which cuts both ways: faster gains, but also a faster path toward either floor if the trade moves against you.

Neither risk rule scales with the leverage setting itself. Max. Drawdown is a fixed dollar floor set at account creation. The Daily Loss Limit uses your daily reset balance, including reserved collateral but excluding unrealized PnL, and adjusts for non-trading transfers. Current equity, including unrealized PnL, is checked against both applicable floors. Increasing position size increases the dollar impact of a price move; changing leverage alone does not change PnL on a fixed quantity.
See [Loss Limits](/vest-capital/loss-limits.md) for the full mechanics of both.

**Funding is paid between holders of long and short positions and is not an exchange fee.**
Funding helps keep the perpetual’s price close to the underlying asset’s index price.
* When funding is **positive**, longs pay shorts.
* When funding is **negative**, shorts pay longs.

Positive funding makes longs more expensive to hold and rewards shorts, encouraging selling that can bring an overpriced perpetual closer to its index price. Negative funding creates the opposite incentive, encouraging buying when the perpetual trades at a discount.
Funding is calculated throughout the hour and **settled hourly**. It combines a market-specific base interest rate with a premium that reflects demand for long or short exposure.

For markets with a nonzero base interest rate, base interest can continue during weekends and trading locks while the market remains listed. CME futures have **zero base interest**, so their funding comes from the premium component.
The hourly rate is calculated as:
I = Annual interest rate × H / (365 × 24)
Hourly funding rate = [P + clamp(I - P, -K × I, +K × I)] / H
Where:
* **P** is the average premium index over the preceding hour.
* **H** is the normalization interval in hours.
* **I** is the interest rate for that normalization interval.
* **K** is the clamp multiplier, set to **1 for all markets**.
* **clamp** limits the adjustment to the range between `-K × I` and `+K × I`.

Futures classification follows the underlying price source: markets whose reference price comes from CME futures use the futures interest rate. An index-linked stock or ETF does not become a futures market merely because it tracks an index.
The normalization interval scales the calculation; payments are still settled hourly. The clamp limits the adjustment, not the final funding rate.
For CME futures, `I = 0`, so the clamp adjustment is zero and the formula simplifies to:
Hourly funding rate = P / H

Assume a **$1.25 million NQ position**, valued at the index price, with an average premium index of **0.12%**. NQ is a CME index futures market, so it uses a **0% annual interest rate** and a **48-hour normalization interval**.
Interval interest = 0%
Clamp size = 1 × 0% = 0%
Clamped adjustment = 0%
Hourly funding rate = 0.12% / 48
The funding payment uses position notional at the **index price**, not the mark price:
Hourly payment = Position notional × Hourly funding rate

A long position pays **$31.25** for that hour; a short position of the same size receives **$31.25**. The $1.25 million is position notional, not margin deposited. Changing leverage without changing the position size does not change the funding payment.

Assume a **$1 million BTC position**, valued at the index price, with an average premium index of **0.12%**. Crypto uses a **10.95% annual interest rate**, a **24-hour normalization interval**, and **K = 1**.
Interval interest = 10.95% × 24 / 8,760 = 0.03%
Unclamped adjustment = 0.03% - 0.12% = -0.09%
Clamped adjustment = clamp(-0.09%, -0.03%, +0.03%)
Hourly funding rate = (0.12% - 0.03%) / 24

The clamp limits the adjustment from `-0.09%` to `-0.03%`; it does not cap the final funding rate. A long position pays **$37.50** for that hour, and a short position of the same size receives **$37.50**.
The premium index compares simulated buy and sell execution prices with the index price:
Premium index =
[max(Buy impact price - Index price, 0)
- max(Index price - Sell impact price, 0)]
/ Index price
Impact prices are the average execution prices for a simulated order sized at `$100 / market initial margin ratio`. Both buy and sell orders must be fully fillable for a sample to count.

Deposits fund your **Primary Account**. Which methods are available, and which networks you can use, depends on how you signed up.
**Funded Accounts cannot receive deposits.** Deposits only go to your Primary Account. See [Vest Capital](/vest-capital/overview.md) for how Funded Accounts are capitalized instead.
Three ways to fund your account:
* **Direct USDC transfer** — send USDC to your account's deposit address on **Base or Arbitrum One**.
* **Fund with Crypto** — send USDC to the deposit address shown on Base or Arbitrum One. Handled by **Relay** directly through **Privy**.
* **Fund with Card** — buy crypto directly with a card or other accepted fiat payment method, converted into your account balance.
For direct transfers and Fund with Crypto, **only send the exact asset shown, on the network shown, to the address shown.** Sending anything else may result in loss of funds.
**1 USDC** per transaction, across all methods and account types.

**Sending less than 1 USDC directly on-chain** (outside the Deposit button flow) **may result in loss of funds.** Deposits below the minimum cannot be initiated from the Deposit button. Always use the in-platform flow rather than sending USDC to your deposit address manually unless you're confident in the amount and network.
Deposits are almost instant in the vast majority of cases for direct USDC transfers.
If a deposit doesn't appear in your balance right away:
Go to the Deposit section and look for a **Process Deposit** button. This manually finalizes a deposit that's pending confirmation.
If Process Deposit isn't there, refresh the page. On-chain confirmations can take a few minutes depending on network conditions.
If the balance still hasn't updated, clear your browser cache, refresh, and log back in.
If the deposit still isn't showing after the above, reach out via **Intercom** or email [**support@vestmarkets.com**](mailto:support@vestmarkets.com) with your transaction details.

Withdrawals move USDC from your **Primary Account** to an external wallet address.

**Withdrawal is not the same as Claim Profit.** Claim Profit moves profit from a Live Funded Account to your Primary Account. Withdrawal moves USDC from your Primary Account out to an external wallet. Two distinct flows with different limits and processing times — see Claim Profit if you're looking to take profit off a Funded Account.
From your Primary Account, start a withdrawal by pressing the Withdraw button.
Manually enter the destination wallet address, choose the chain, and enter the amount. Supported chains are shown at the point of withdrawal.
Once submitted, a withdrawal **cannot be reversed or recovered.** Confirm the details are correct before sending.
The platform does not automatically route funds to the address you originally deposited from. Double-check the destination address and chain before confirming.
* **Minimum withdrawal: 1 USDC.**

* **$50,000 rolling 24-hour limit.** Withdrawals process instantly until your rolling 24-hour total reaches $50,000. Any withdrawal that pushes your rolling total over that amount is subject to a 24-hour processing period.

**Example:** you withdraw $50,000, then request a further $1,000 within the same 24-hour window. That second request is subject to a 24-hour processing period, since it takes your rolling total over the $50,000 threshold.
This limit applies to withdrawals only. It does not apply to Claim Profit from Funded Accounts.
Supported chains are displayed at the point of withdrawal.
The **Withdrawals** tab on your Portfolio page shows every withdrawal: type, USDC amount, status, date and time, and on-chain transaction ID.
**My withdrawal shows as filled but hasn't arrived.**

Check the status in the Withdrawals tab. If it shows **Processing** or **Filled** and the funds haven't arrived, contact support via **Intercom** or email [**support@vestmarkets.com**](mailto:support@vestmarkets.com) with:
* The transaction ID
* The destination chain
* The amount
**Is anything extra required for a first withdrawal?**
No. First and subsequent withdrawals are handled identically. All withdrawals process as USDC to the wallet address and chain you specify.

Perpetual contracts are derivatives that never expire. Unlike traditional futures contracts, they can be held indefinitely. Funding payments are made hourly to help converge the contract's price to the underlying asset's Index price.
Coming from CME futures? See [Cross Margin & Leverage](/trading/cross-margin-and-leverage.md) for Micro E-mini and E-mini equivalents, order-entry quantities, and a worked example.

SettlementUSDC-margined, linear 1:1 contracts
Position LimitsNo position or order size limits
Margin RequirementsMarket-specific
Maintenance MarginHalf of the initial margin requirement
Mark Price is used for liquidation. Mid Price is used for unrealized PnL and account balances.
The real-time market price of the underlying asset.
During market hours, Vest derives the index price from an aggregate of exchanges such as NASDAQ, NYSE, CME, and BlueOcean ATS.
Both the Mark Price and Index Price are constrained by threshold bands to safeguard against manipulation and prevent erratic price movements during periods of extreme market volatility.

Perpetual contracts tied to CME futures undergo a periodic roll to the next front-month contract. Rolls are executed during the CME maintenance window on the dates listed below. Prices, including index price, entry prices, liquidation prices, are all adjusted internally at the time of the roll so there is no impact to P\&L, position value or jumps in the prices.
**ES-PERP (E-mini S\&P 500)**

Basis limits restrict how far a perpetual contract’s trading price can deviate from its Index Price. They function similarly to limit-up and limit-down rules, with upper and lower price boundaries defined relative to the Index Price.
The **basis** is the difference between the perpetual contract price and the Index Price, expressed in basis points:
Basis (bps) = ((Perpetual Price − Index Price) / Index Price) × 10,000
A positive basis means the perpetual is trading above the Index Price; a negative basis means it is trading below.
Each market has a specified basis limit. Trades cannot execute above the upper boundary or below the lower boundary. Trading within the permitted band can continue.
Basis limits help prevent excessive price dislocations during volatile or low-liquidity conditions.

If your account has a DLL, the daily reset boundary is **20:00 ET**. The reset balance includes reserved collateral but **excludes unrealized PnL**. Your daily floor is **reset balance × (1 − your DLL rate) + net non-trading transfers since reset**. Current account equity, including unrealized PnL, is checked against this floor.

For example, a $25,000 reset balance with a 4% DLL sets a $24,000 daily floor before transfers. Withdrawals lower this floor by the full amount; non-trading credits raise it by the full amount. Equity falling below either applicable loss floor closes the account permanently. The separate Max. Drawdown floor still applies. Instant Accounts and the “No Daily Loss Limit” option have no DLL.
**Breaching either rule results in immediate, permanent account closure.** There is no warning and no grace period. You would need to purchase a new Funded Account to trade again.
A **fixed floor**, set once when your account is created. It never moves.
* Profits don't raise it.
* Losses don't lower it further.
* Calculated as a percentage of your **starting capital,** not your current balance.
If your account equity drops below the floor at any point, intraday or otherwise, the account closes immediately.

* Daily floor = reset balance × (1 − rate) + net non-trading transfers since reset. Before transfers, this is 97% of reset balance at 3%, or 96% at 4%.

**Max. Drawdown** is fixed at **$23,500** as an equity floor from day one: $25,000 minus the $1,500 loss allowance (6% of starting capital). The floor never moves, regardless of how the account performs.

Daily Loss Limit recalculates every day. If your reset balance is $25,000, the floor is $25,000 × 0.96 = $24,000 before transfers. An open position with $2,000 of unrealized profit raises current equity to $27,000 but does not raise the reset balance or the daily floor. If your realized balance, including reserved collateral, is $27,000 at the next reset, the new floor is $27,000 × 0.96 = $25,920.

A $500 withdrawal after a $25,000 reset lowers the DLL floor from $24,000 to $23,500. The full withdrawal is deducted from the floor, even if the account has made profits since reset. A $500 non-trading credit instead raises it to $24,500. The separate Max. Drawdown floor stays fixed.

Both limits are active at once. Before transfers in this example, the Daily Loss Limit floor ($24,000) sits above the Max. Drawdown floor ($23,500). Equity falling below either applicable floor closes the account; equality alone does not breach a limit.
